Tiny House Croissant Is a Smart Tiny Living Solution Designed to Grow Over Time
22 photos
Photo: Mobi House
The deliciously-named tiny house Croissant is purposely meant to grow, not in the sense that the unit itself can expand, but that it can easily connect to one or even more similar modules from the same line. This is classic home on wheels design combined with modern modular design, and the result is one of the smartest, most efficient solutions available on the market right now.
The best thing about this whole concept is that you start things off with a fully furnished and equipped tiny home that’s ready for you to move into. In other words, this tiny abode is a self-contained full-time residence all on its own, and it’s perfectly fine if it stays that way. It’s strictly the owner’s option whether they want to add one or more modules over time, and exactly when to do that. Each new unit means added floor space and complex functionality without the hassle.
One of the key points here is that these units are purposely designed and built from to match and to be easy to connect. This is the main idea behind the Modul Line by the Poland-based Mobi House. This new line is all about combining mobility with flexibility. Customers can start with a single module and then add more units at a future time in order to expand their overall living time, but they also have the option to buy a ready-made set from the start.
The line is comprised of two primary platforms, the Modul Sunrise, which has the layout and the functionality of a fully functional home, and the Modul Sunset, with a double bedroom layout that offers additional accommodation. Modul Sunrise boasts 16.2 square meters (174 square feet) of floor space, and Modul Sunset offers 11.87 square meters (127 square feet). Each one can accommodate up to four people, and they both come with a tiny built-in terrace.
Photo: Mobi House The possible combinations between these two flexible units are numerous. The “parallel connection” option places two or many more modules side by side, it’s very easy to set up, and it allows virtually endless expansion. The “Z connection” option is based on a zigzag pattern that leaves certain empty spaces which can be further used to add tiny terraces or other structures.
Lastly, the “L connection” pattern is a classic option where the modules are linked at a right angle. This option allows for a more creative approach, also creating additional space for a small garden or something similar. In each case, owners can start with how many modules they want and are free to add more units whenever they wish – this is what makes the Modul Line such a smart, practical solution both in terms of money and space.
It’s also important to note that modules are just as easy to disassemble as they are to connect. This is another huge advantage in terms of flexibility, as it allows owner to move or even resell one or some of the units over time with zero hassle and without impacting the main residence.
Tiny house Croissant is a custom-styled version of Modul Sunrise, the main-residence platform from the Modul Line. The smart layout is divided into a central open lounge with complex functionality, a compact kitchen at one end, a bathroom next to it, and a sleeping loft above. The convertible sofa means that up to four people can be accommodate inside Tiny Croissant (two downstairs and two in the loft), and the home comes fully equipped for year-round comfort.
Photo: Mobi House Style-wise, Tiny Croissant showcases a bolder approach with industrial-style accents and a moody, darker ambiance. It’s very different than the standard Scandinavian aesthetic typically found in tiny homes from this European brand, and it instantly makes this model look contemporary and more sophisticated.
All the cabinetry throughout the house is black, matching the window frames, but the striking effect is toned down by the soft yellow textiles and the warm, natural tone of the wood paneling. This combination between wood walls and black furniture is actually very well-balanced, and the soft yellow accents add just the right cozy touch to keep this palette from becoming too harsh. The effect is welcoming and relaxing, but also a bit edgy.
Tiny Croissant is not only a custom version, but also a fully-equipped home, ready for someone to move in. The kitchen comes with a sink, an induction stove, a fridge, and a range hood – only the essentials, since this is an ultra-compact kitchen designed to fit in one end of the layout, right next to the bathroom. The bathroom is also small, but it’s so well-furnished and styled that it looks almost luxurious.
It’s fitted with a shower cabin, a sink with a small vanity, and a conventional toilet. The backlit mirror, the towel rack, and the full-height closet for extra storage are some of the details that take this bathroom from basic to elegant. Plus, the aesthetic follows the main guidelines of the rest of the house, including the black cabinets, the natural wood paneling, and discrete lighting, for a cohesive look.
Photo: Mobi House Tiny Croissant comes fully prepped for connection to electricity, water, and sewage utilities, and is also equipped for all-season thermal comfort. This includes air conditioning with a heating function, heating mats, and an additional heater.
Built for full mobility, this 6.6-meter (21.6 feet) home comes on a THM 660 Lift &Go chassis by MH Trailers (the brand developed by Mobi House specifically for tiny house trailers, and the official trailer supplier in Poland). The Lift &Go is an innovation that allows the trailer to be easily detached from the tiny house after delivery, which offers a series of advantages linked to greater flexibility for the owner.
Large windows and overall expansive glazing are a very important element of this design. Although compact, Tiny Croissant feels a lot bigger thanks to its modern, open interior, plus large windows that open the space further. The rear entrance with a transom window above the door acts as a secondary entrance (the main one, also with glass doors, leads into the kitchen/dining area) and it connects the lounge with the mini built-in terrace.
The custom cabinetry in the lounge and beyond is what makes this tiny house very practical despite the size limitations. Most of the lounge cabinets are mounted on the wall, which saves a great deal of space, and then continue with a full-height unit connected to the corner sofa, which provides easy-to-reach storage.
Photo: Mobi House Next to it, another ingenious piece of furniture acts as a smart, more versatile alternative to a classic table. It takes up minimal floor space and it serves both as a breakfast bar (with room for two bar stools) and as a home office desk with an excellent placement.
Since a staircase would have changed the layout entirely, the builder opted for a basic ladder instead – it takes up zero floor space, as it can be stored horizontally on the lounge wall when not in use.
Overall, Tiny Croissant feels like a light-filled sanctuary surrounded by natural views, which makes it seem more spacious. As part of the Modul Line, it can be enjoyed as a perfect home on its own, but it can also be connected to a smaller Modul Sunset unit for additional accommodation, or to another Modul Sunrise unit – there are countless options for future growth and expansion, and it can all start with this single, smart home.

Monumental ‘90s Megayacht Emerges After a Decade, Asking for a Whopping $86M
23 photos
Photo: IYC
It irrupted in the early 1990s, breaking all rules and proving the impossible, it stayed hidden for almost a decade, and now it’s back, looking just as dazzling as it did the first day. Forever an icon and one of the boldest superyachts ever built (both in terms of design and propulsion), Zeus is true to its name: a deity of superyachts, looking for a new owner.
Few superyachts deserve the iconic status of Zeus – one of the most incredible luxury yachts of all time on all levels. Right now, this masterpiece is back in the spotlight after almost a full decade of mystery. It has never been chartered in its 35 years of existence, and its most recent (and current) owner chose to keep it away from the spotlight since 2017, when it purchased it. Properly maintained and refitted during all these years, Zeus has re-emerged in full glory.
It was one of the superstars of this year’s Monaco Yacht Show in September, joining the lineup for the first time in almost ten years. It was also one of the most expensive superyachts on display, asking for a whopping Є77 million ($86 million) – an enormous price for a yacht from the ‘90s, but fully justifiable, given its unrivaled iconic status.
Zeus was originally named Eco, a wordplay that hinted at the metaphorical meaning of the Spanish word “echo”, and also stood for “Empresa de Comunicaciones Orbitales”, a news channel founded in 1988. The man behind this news channel was the same behind the futuristic yacht, namely Emilio Azcárraga, the Mexican media mogul dubbed “El Tigre” (The Tiger).
Photo: IYC Azcárraga was compared to Rupert Murdoch, but many believe that what he did for the Mexican media (television in particular) is far greater and pioneering. His life and his personality were just as grandiose as his media empire, so they naturally fitted a collection of radically different, bold luxury yachts unlike anything else on the market at that time. The media mogul started small, with a basic 36-meter CRN motor yacht (named Caribe III) in the ‘70s.
From there, he moved to owning twin superyachts built at the same time according to his specifications. Azteca and Paraiso were the first manifestations of Azcarraga’s futuristic vision and opulent taste – built by Feadship, they were dubbed “the greenhouse yachts” because locals actually believed they were giant greenhouses, not yachts . That was mainly because of the unusual glazing on the top decks, which was unprecedented at the time.
A striking glass design would also later become one of the most revolutionary features of the futuristic Eco. As revolutionary as they were, Azteca and Paraiso only paved the way for what would become Azcarraga’s masterpiece: the 74.5-meter (244 feet) superyacht that took years and considerable effort to build because it was such an unusual project, and one that literally developed organically, taking a life of its own.
Azcárraga's original brief changed tremendously and eventually became what was known as Eco – the 1991 megayacht that revolutionized everything that existed in that size category at the time. El Tigre only got to enjoy this masterpiece for a few years, and even spent the final moments of his life onboard Eco. After he passed away in 1997, Eco was purchased by another famous, ultra-rich owner: Larry Ellison.
Photo: IYC Ellison renamed it Katana and made important tweaks to the megayacht, completed by the same original designer. Ellison would go on to own a series of custom-built superyachts based on his own vision, leaving the ’91 Eco behind. In 2004, it was sold to British entrepreneur Aidan Barclay and renamed Enigma. The current owner (reportedly the Monaco-based real estate mogul John Christodoulou) purchased it in 2017, renaming it Zeus.
Azcárraga brought the vision and the money for this masterpiece, but the real genius behind it is Martin Francis, the multi-talented designer that led the entire project (exterior and interior), which is a monumental task in its own. It wasn’t a smooth process, like today’s superyachts that follow a precise brief and are completed in two years, but things worked out in the end, resulting in something bigger (literally and figuratively) than the owner himself first planned.
Zeus became a milestone for almost everyone involved in the process of bringing it to life, from Martin Francis (this was his first motor yacht) and François Zuretti (who had never worked on a yacht interior until then), to the entire team of young designers and architects, some of whom would eventually become iconic names in the industry (most notably, Espen Oeino).
Azcarraga’s first two custom superyachts were built by the Dutch giant Feadship, but for Eco, he tapped Blohm+Voss, a German shipyard, specifically for its experience with gas turbine-powered high-speed vessels. The Blohm+Voss shipyard was later acquired by the Lurssen Group, the biggest German builder of superyachts, where it remains active as a distinctive brand.
The yacht was monumental in size and groundbreaking in design – the unique superstructure with curved panoramic windows became the most recognizable feature of Zeus, one that was never replicated on another yacht and that is just as iconic to this day. The convex-built windows that make Zeus look so striking both inside and out were apparently inspired by French buses.
Photo: IYC For the interior, Azcarraga wanted an Art Deco aesthetic, and the famous François Zuretti worked with Francis to create something that remains iconic to this day. Even 35 years later, Zeus sports the same original interior design, only with careful upgrades such as stone restoration, leatherwork, and new carpets in the guest area (added in 2025).
The massive 1,150 GT volume allowed for a six-stateroom configuration that can accommodate up to 15 guests, attended by an equally massive crew of 21. The elevated Panoramic Salon is one of the most impressive living spaces onboard.
The giant aft deck (later transformed into a basketball court for Ellison) was originally meant to house an impressive selection of toys, including a Maule turbo-prop float plane, a luxurious Riva Aquarama, and even a Harley Davidson.
From the start, Zeus didn’t boast just a radically innovative design, but also one of the boldest technical approaches to propulsion, at a time when that was rare. The high-speed gas turbine option was chosen in order to allow greater speeds of up to 30 knots.
Photo: IYC The complete propulsion system would combine a central GE LM1600 gas turbine (Zeus became the launch customer for this turbine) driving a booster jet (the KaMeWa waterjet was the largest-ever built at that time) with classic twin diesel engines driving wing jets.
In addition to this, the use of underwater foil was also revolutionary at the time, allowing for smooth cruising even at the exceptional speed of 35 knots. Imagine a behemoth megayacht of over 200 feet speeding at 35 knots and still maintaining a vibration-free experience for the onboard guests.
This unique, high-performance propulsion system combined with hydrofoil technology provides up to 28,5000 combined horsepower, resulting in a maximum speed of 35 knots. At an economical speed of just 12 knots, Zeus turns into a long-range beast capable of covering up to 4,000 nautical miles.
To these outstanding capabilities of the original design, subsequent refits added premium zero-speed stabilizers, major work completed on the machinery, waterjet, and navigation, plus communications refit work leading to a fully upgraded bridge.
Photo: IYC When he was still alive and well, Azcárraga tested the yacht’s long-range capabilities by cruising extensively on both sides of the Atlantic. He even traveled with a small tanker named Eco Supporter (similar to today’s shadow yachts built for massive megayachts) that enabled the refueling of the gas turbine during extended cruises.
Back in 1991, Eco was a total disruptor and a pioneer. Today, it remains a huge part of modern yacht design, and ultimately a collector’s item – one that is fully operable and worth more than some of the best brand-new superyacht on the market.

5 Euro 7-Seaters From the 2000s That Combined Practicality With Hot-Hatch Power
11 photos
Photo: Stellantis N.V.
During the 2000s, when MPVs - Europe’s equivalent to minivans – were not yet rendered extinct by SUVs, some carmakers decided that offering practicality and comfort wasn’t enough, so they fitted several models with genuine performance engines.
I don’t know about you, but for me, it’s often mind-blowing that two decades have passed since the 2000s. Yes, I know, logic and the calendar should be enough to prevent such thoughts, but that was an epic decade for anything car-related. It was a decade that passed way too fast and one that I seriously miss, especially in this boring era of electrification.
From hot hatches to high-performance, V10-powered sedans and supercars that began blurring the lines between ‘super’ and ‘hyper,’ the 2000s had it all.
In Europe, the decade also gave family-oriented enthusiasts the following five MPVs with seven-seat capabilities and supreme comfort, coupled with genuine performance engines that were either shared with hot hatches, matched or far exceeded the capabilities of the era’s most potent hatchbacks.
2000 Volkswagen Sharan / Seat Alhambra / Ford Galaxy 2.8 V6 Photo: VW AG Originally launched in 1996, the Sharan was the product of a joint venture between Volkswagen and the Ford Motor Company’s European division, one that also spawned the nearly identical Ford Galaxy and Seat Alhambra.
All three sister models shared the same list of motors throughout their lifespan, including some potent gasoline V6 units, of which the most powerful became available for the 2000 model year.
That year, the seven-seat MPV trio received a facelift and a revised flagship engine offering in the shape of VW’s 2.8-liter V6.
Photo: SEAT Based on the epic VR6 engine architecture, the unit was upgraded with a freer-flowing 24-valve cylinder head that pushed output to 201 hp.
Closely related to the unit that powered the Golf Mk4 V6 4Motion, the motor gave the MPVs plenty of power for a spirited driving experience and soothed the driver’s ears with its menacing soundtrack.
In terms of actual performance, the V6-powered MPVs weren’t exactly hot-hatch fast, as they took about 10 seconds to reach 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill, but they still delivered performance and quickness well above the MPV segment’s average.
2002 Renault Espace IV 3.5 V6 Photo: Renault S.A. Launched in 2002, the fourth-generation of the Espace , wasn’t the prettiest iteration of Renault’s flagship MPV.
However, when equipped with the most potent gasoline engine available, the Espace, which was also available with three rows of seats in Grand Espace trim, was one of the most spectacular offerings of the segment.
That engine was a 3.5-liter V6 codenamed V4Y by Renault, but it was far better known by enthusiasts by its Nissan internal code: VQ35DE.
Photo: Renault S.A. Yes, you read that right, the fourth-gen Espace was available with a variant of the Nissan-built engine that powered performance rides like the 350Z.
While no version of the engine family was ever fitted to a hot hatch , with 241 hp on tap in V4Y guise, it gave the MPV unquestionable hot-hatch power.
Able to reach 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill in a solid eight seconds - about as quick as the 2005-08 Ford Fiesta ST150, the V6-powered Espace remains one of the quirkiest factory-built sleepers of the 2000s.
2005 Opel Zafira OPC / Vauxhall Zafira VXR (B) Photo: Stellantis N.V. The original Zafira, known as the Zafira A, was co-developed with Porsche and while it didn’t have true Porsche performance DNA, it was available in high-performance OPC (or VXR, in the UK) guise, making it one of the most spectacular factory-built MPVs of its era.
Naturally, when the second-generation Zafira B was launched, the OPC/VXR version returned and became even more spectacular.
Like its predecessor, the second-gen OPC/VXR variant came with a distinct body kit and suspension upgrades that made it look more aggressive than the standard Zafira.
Photo: Stellantis N.V. More importantly, it was powered by a 2.0-liter, 16-valve turbocharged inline-four DOHC gasoline engine that delivered 240 hp.
That motor, codenamed Z20LEH was genuine performance-oriented unit shared with the Astra H OPC/VXR three-door hot hatch.
While obviously heavier, the Zafira OPC/VXR could still accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (97 kph) in 7.8 seconds, which was a whisker from what the Ford Focus ST170 hot hatch could achieve.
Moreover, with a top speed of 144 mph (231 kph), the Zafira B OPC/VXR was marketed as the fastest MPV available in Europe at the time.
2006 Ford S-Max 2.5T Photo: Ford Motor Co. The next MPV on our list comes with Ford badges, but before you point out that it’s an American carmaker, remember that it was conceived by Ford Europe in, well, Europe where the model was also assembled.
Introduced in 2006 as a compact MPV, the S-Max was well received on the old continent, wining the European Car of the Year in 2007.
Available with a third row of seats, albeit small child seats, the compact MPV could be purchased, in typical 2000s fashion, with a high-performance engine under the hood.
{fulimg8}
That engine was the Volvo-sourced 2.5-liter turbocharged inline-five codenamed B5254T3, the exact same engine that powered the Mk2 Focus ST hot hatch.
Rated at 217 hp, the motor enabled the compact MPV to reach 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill in an impressive 7.8 seconds.
While that was slower than the Mk2 Focus ST by about a second, it was more than enough to make the S-Max feel more like a hot hatch than the goofy-looking, family-oriented MPV it actually was.
2007 Mercedes-Benz R63 AMG Photo: Mercedes-Benz AG The final entry on our list is a bit of an oddball. Marketed by Mercedes-Benz as a grand sports tourer, the R-Class was actually classified as an MPV even though it looked like it sat on the border between a conventional wagon and a minivan.
If you’re a Mercedes fan, you know that the R-Class was quite the epic failure for the German brand, but it also spawned one of the rarest, most unconventional AMG models ever produced.
Dubbed R63 AMG , the model was only available throughout the 2007 model year and went down as the craziest family-oriented, seven-seater (optional configuration) ever produced in Europe.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz AG Under the hood, the R63 hid the iconic M156 , a handcrafted V8 masterpiece that produced no less than 503 hp.
Shared with all the flagship AMG-tuned performance offerings in Mercedes-Benz’s portofolio, the naturally aspirated 6.2-liter powerhouse enabled the R-Class to reach 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill in 4.6 seconds.
While the engine was never used in a hot hatch, it gave the quirky MPV some serious power that didn’t just match, but exceeded what even the most potent hot hatches of the 2000s had on tap.

5 of the Most Underrated Supercars From the 1990s
11 photos
Photo: Venturi
The 1990s saw the introduction of many iconic supercars that are still very much relevant three decades later. However, several impressive models which never quite shone under the mainstream spotlight have been unfairly forgotten.
When enthusiasts think about an iconic 1990s supercar, they usually think about the McLaren F1, the Ferrari 512 TR or F50, the Lamborghini Diablo , or the Dodge Viper.
While those legendary models were without a doubt epic, they were not the only impressive supercars that hit the streets during that exciting decade.
Often left out of the conversations about 1990s supercar legends, the following five models never reached the highest levels of notoriety, but, since they still look and perform terrifically even by current standards, these underrated machines deserve a second look.
Venturi 400 GT Photo: Venturi French carmakers have produced many legendary vehicles throughout the decades, but let’s be honest: when it comes to 1990s supercars, few will think about a model designed and produced in France.
Nevertheless, a small French manufacturer which, almost certainly won’t ring any familiar bells, did produce an awesome supercar during the 1990s -albeit one that few still remember.
That French manufacture was Venturi and the supercar, often nicknamed the French F40 , was the 400 GT.
Photo: Venturi This impressive supercar which obviously lived up to its nickname started life as a thoroughbred race car built specifically for the track, but morphed into a fully-road legal model in 1994.
Designed in-house from the ground up by Venturi, the 400 GT was a RWD mid-engine beast powered by a custom 3.0-liter PRV V6, originally developed by Peugeot, Renault, and Volvo.
Equipped with twin turbos , the engine produced a little over 400 hp, allowing the 400 GT to reach 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill in about four seconds.
The quickest production car ever built in France at the time of its introduction, the 400 GT was manufactured in a limited series of approximately 15 units, which makes it the rarest model on this list.
Vector M12 Photo: Vector Back in the late 1980s, a small yet ambitious American startup dubbed the Vector Aeromotive Corporation introduced the W8, a futuristic, aircraft-inspired supercar capable of mind-blowing performance figures.
Since the company was plagued by financial constraints, the W8 was only produced in 22 units and never quite got the credit it deserved.
Vector went through a hostile takeover but continued to produce cars and after unveiling the successor of the W8 in 1993 in the shape of the WX-3 concept , the company introduced its second production model in 1995.
Photo: Vector Christened M12, the supercar was loosely based on the WX-3 concept in terms of styling, but when it came to the mechanicals, it borrowed chassis components and the powertrain from the Lamborghini Diablo.
Designed by the great Peter Stevens, who also penned the McLaren F1, the M12 was not as insane nor as bespoke as the W8, but still kicked some serious supercar behind.
Powered by a 5.7-liter Lambo V12 rated at 492 hp, the supercar assembled in Florida could easily accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 4.8 seconds and reach a top speed of 189 mph (304 kph).
Produced in around 17 units, the M12 never reached the same level of American supercar greatness as the Dodge Viper, but remains impressive nearly three decades after the last unit hit the streets.
Jaguar XJR-15 Photo: Jaguar Cars Unlike today, when electric powertrains and brutally minimalistic design are seen as the future of the company, back in the 1990s, Jaguar was building timeless automotive works of art.
Most enthusiasts will remember the XJ220 as Jaguar’s halo 1990s production model, but that wasn’t the only impressive supercar that the company conceived during that decade.
Unleashed on public roads a couple of years before the XJ220, the XJR-15 was Jaguar’s first contribution to the 1990s supercar segment.
Photo: Jaguar Cars Co-developed by JaguarSport and Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR) , the XJR-15 was based on the underpinnings of the Le Mans-winning XJR-9 and featured a custom carbon-Kevlar body designed by the same Peter Stevens.
Power came from a mid-mounted 6.0-liter naturally aspirated Jaguar V12 that delivered 450 hp to the rear wheels through a five-speed manual.
Capable of reaching 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill in 3.9 seconds, the XJR-15 was one of the quickest, most impressive production cars in the world at the time of its introduction.
However, due to a low-volume production run and the introduction of the XJ220, it never reached the level of popularity it deserved.
Cizeta V16T Photo: Cizeta It’s hard to argue that Italy gave the world some of the most impressive supercars during the 1990s. But while Ferrari and Lamborghini’s offerings became legends, they weren’t the only impressive supercars built in Italy during that decade.
In 1988, former Lamborghini designer Claudio Zampolli teamed up with Oscar-winning music composer Giorgio Moroder and founded Cizeta Automobili, which went on to produce the V16T.
Designed by legendary stylist Marcello Gandini and loosely inspired by the initial Lamborghini Diablo prototype, this supercar became the first and only production model of the 1990s to feature a V16 engine.
Photo: Cizeta The unconventional motor, which was mounted transversally behind the cockpit , was created by basically combining two Lamborghini V8s into a single 6.0-liter unit capable of producing 540 hp.
Thanks to that potent motor, the V16T could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in a little under four seconds and reach a top speed of 204 mph (328 kph).
Because of financial constrains only eleven units were ever produced and with no proper marketing budget, the V16T never shone as bright as it unquestionably deserved.
Nevertheless, the V16-powered beast remains one of the most exciting supercars produced during the 1990s.
Bugatti EB110 Photo: Bugatti When people talk about the first modern Bugatti, they usually go straight to the Veyron, often forgetting about the EB110.
While not as obscure and underrated as the other entries on this list, the first and only Italian Bugatti to reach production is often forgotten by enthusiasts these days.
The EB110 made its public debut on September 15, 1991 in Paris, celebrating 110 years since the birth of company founder Ettore Bugatti .
Photo: Bugatti While it remained a French brand and was unveiled in the country’s capital city, the EB110 was 100% Italian, being conceived and assembled in Modena.
Designed by a team of legendary stylists and engineers which included the likes of Marcello Gandini, Paolo Stanzani, and Nicola Materazzi, the EB110 was the first production car to feature a quad-turbocharged engine.
A 3.5-liter V12 capable of either 553 hp in the GT trim or 603 in the Super Sport , the engine worked together with a permanent AWD system that made the EB110 one of the best-handling supercars of its era.
Produced in 139 units, this Italian Bugatti may still be overlooked, yet it remains one of the most impressive supercars to reach production during the 1990s.

5 of the Rarest American High-Performance Road Cars From the 1960s
16 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's
The 1960s saw American carmakers unleash a long list of raw high-performance versions of their production models. But while most were produced in large numbers, some were build in extremely low figures, making them iconic holy grails.
In more ways than one, the 1960s was a transformative decade in American history. From the civil rights movement to landing on the moon, that period was marked by huge leaps for society.
For the local automotive industry, the 1960s marked the beginning of a short yet memorable era of untamed performance.
Whether on the world’s most legendary race tracks, local drag strips, an empty stretches of public roads, American cars were setting new standards for factory-built performance.
The decade saw the introduction of many impressive high-performance machines built in the US. But while some sold in huge numbers, some special-order brutes quietly earned their place in automotive history books with their impressive performance prowess and rarity.
1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty – 14 units Photo: Mecum Auctions Pontiac is widely credited with kickstarting the muscle car craze in 1964, when it added the GTO package to the intermediate Tempest/LeMans line.
However, a year before that legendary muscle car was born, the GM division introduced a special-order, drag-strip-oriented beast that packed a whole lot of muscle into a full-size chassis.
That beast was none other than the 1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty, an ultra-rare performance icon that earned the nickname Swiss Cheese ."
Photo: Mecum Auctions That name came from the fac that each of the fourteen units built was put on an extensive weight-saving diet which, apart from the removal of features such as carpeting and sound insulation, included over 100 large holes being punched into the frame rails.
The epic full-size coupe was powered by a race-bred, 421-ci (6.9-liter) Super Duty V8 that Pontiac rated at 405 hp. However, the engine was allegedly capable of close to 500 hp.
Theoretically street legal, the 1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty was one of the most insane drag-strip specials produced during the golden age of muscle.
1966 Dodge Coronet HEMI Sedan – 5 units Photo: Mecum Auctions The Chrysler Corporation introduced the now-legendary 426 HEMI V8 in 1964 as a competition-only motor conceived to give the Plymouth and Dodge brands the edge in NASCAR.
However, the competition’s governing body modified the rulebook a year later, forcing the corporation to develop a street version of the engine and make it available in its production models.
That led Plymouth and Dodge to add the 426 street HEMI as an option for many of its cars for the 1966 model year.
Photo: Mecum Auctions While most enthusiasts added the HEMI option to a two-door coupe, a very few decided to add the Elephant engine to the Coronet sedan.
The exact number of HEMI-powered Coronet sedans produced in 1966 was five, all of which delivered with the upscale Deluxe trim.
One of the rarest, most intriguing American performance models of the 1960s, the Coronet HEMI sedan looked just like a conventional Coronet Deluxe, but with 425-hp on tap, it became one of the most impressive factory-built sleepers ever produced.
1966 Shelby GT350 Convertible – 4 units Photo: Mecum Auctions For 1965, the first full model year for the Mustang, which was introduced halfway through the 1964 model year, Ford partnered up with Carroll Shelby and his Shelby American crew to transform the model into a genuine performance car.
The result was the Shelby GT350 , a tuned, lightweight variant of the Mustang fastback coupe which immediately proved its worth on the street and the track.
For the 1966 model year, the GT350 returned with several improvements but the story goes that one particular buyer wanted Shelby to add a convertible option to that list of improvements.
Photo: Mecum Auctions That buyer was Bob Shane, a member of the pop group “ The Kingston Trio ,” who was close friends with Carroll Shelby and managed to convince the engineering mastermind to build a drop-top GT350.
Despite the fact that Shelby didn’t initially consider building a convertible version due to chassis rigidity concerns, he went on to build one for Shane anyway, then put together three more to see if how fast he could sell them.
While based on the standard ragtop Mustang, the 1966 GT350 convertible featured all the modifications of its fixed-roof sibling. That meant a tweaked suspension and a 306-hp HiPo K-Code version of the Windsor 289 nestled between its shock towers.
Shelby managed to sell the additional convertibles quite fast, but decided against offering one for the 1967 model year. However, a convertible GT350 finally arrived a year later and was produced in 404 examples.
1967 Dodge Coronet R/T HEMI Convertible – 3 units Photo: Mecum Auctions Dodge and Plymouth continued to offer the Elephant engine for the 1967 model year, but by now, the engine was only available on select two-door models.
The vast majority of buyers who ticked the HEMI option on the ordered sheet purchased a hardtop because the chassis was more rigid than the convertible.
Nevertheless, a few drop-top enthusiasts chose to equip their new rides with the 425-hp Elephant engine.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Of the ragtops sold in 1967 with a HEMI under the hood , the rarest was the Coronet R/T, of which Dodge produced just three units.
Two of them were equipped with a four-speed manual gearbox, while a single one received the 426 HEMI/three-speed Torqueflite automatic powertrain combo.
Today all three 1967 Coronet R/T HEMI Convertibles survive and are considered some of the most sought-after muscle cars ever produced.
1969 Chevrolet Corvette ZL1 – 2 units Photo: RM Sotheby's While GM had a strict ban on motorsport during the latter part of the 1960s, for the 1969 model year, several important Chevy dealers devised a clever scheme to build some uniquely impressive rides through the COPO (Central Office Production Order) fleet-ordering system.
The scheme led to the creation of several Camaros equipped with the L72 427 big-block V8 and the race-bred, all-aluminum ZL1 version .
This resulted in 69 ZL1-equipped Camaros, 50 of which were delivered to Illinois-based Chevy dealer Fred Gibb, while the rest were distributed to other established dealerships throughout the country.
Photo: RM Sotheby's However, apart from the 69 Camaros, Chevy also built two special-order COPO Corvettes equipped with the legendary ZL1.
Rated at only 430 hp on paper, for insurance-related reasons, the aluminum ZL1 engine was actually capable of delivering well over 550 hp when put on a dyno.
With that engine under the hood, the Corvette could run the quarter mile in the low 12-second range in otherwise stock guise.
Today, the ZL1 remains the rarest factory-built Corvette and the two units are some of the most valuable examples of Chevy’s iconic sports car. Three years ago, the orange convertible shown above was auctioned off by RM Sotheby’s, fetching a jaw-dropping $3,140,000.

Tuner Ignores the New GT 4-Door Coupe, Modifies the Heck Out of the Old GT 63 S
7 photos
Photo: Instagram | performmaster
It’s been almost half a year since Mercedes-AMG introduced the all-new GT 4-Door Coupe , with its soulless design, and battery-electric firepower, and this model still hasn’t grown on me. Chances are you may feel the same, but do you think that the Affalterbach brand cares?
That would be a no, obviously, as instead of trying to convince us that this model is worth every penny, despite the quirky design, it has launched a similar-looking electric super crossover. The GT SUV uses the same underpinnings as the new-gen GT 4-Door Coupe, and has a very similar design, so it is not exactly my cup of tea either.
But do you know what the best part of the new GT 4-Door Coupe is? That the old model has started to look a heck of a lot better all of a sudden. You see, the old Mercedes- AMG GT 4-Door Coupe has never been a looker, unlike the demised CLS , which also shared the same MRA construction, just like the W213 E-Class, the W205 C-Class, and the old GLC, among others, but compared to its electric successor, it definitely looks like a winner.
We recently dedicated a few stories to this model for different reasons, and it is now time to put the spotlight on the car pictured in the gallery. As mentioned in the title, you are looking at a Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S, a model that came with 630 horsepower (470 kW/639 ps) straight from the factory, and 664 pound-feet (900 Nm) of torque. That’s how much its familiar bi-turbo 4.0-liter V8 engine produced with no outside intervention.
Photo: Instagram | performmaster The lump was mated to a nine-speed automatic transmission that delivered everything to the 4Matic+ all-wheel drive system. Mercedes-AMG’s old GT 63 S took just 3.2 seconds to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph), and that’s similar to previous-generation supercars. Keep in mind that we are talking about a premium mid-size model with a spacious interior. And it is one that will keep going all the way up to 196 mph (316 kph).
However, this example is a lot quicker. PerformMaster stands behind the modifications, and claims that this machine has a whopping 809 hp (820 ps/603 kW) on tap, and 789 pound-feet (1,070 Nm) of torque. This makes the tuned Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S 179 hp (181 ps/133 kW) and 125 lb-ft (170 Nm) of torque more powerful than the standard one, hence why it is four-tenths of a second faster.
The tuner says that 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) takes just 2.8 seconds in this example, which makes it just 0.1 seconds slower than the Lamborghini Temerario , which is the Raging Bull’s new baby supercar, and a lot quicker than the Temerario’s predecessor, the Huracan, which was made in the same era as the old GT 4-Door Coupe.
To better understand these numbers, we will remind you that the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S E Performance, aka the electrified one, sprints from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph) in just 2.8 seconds, which is identical to this tuned example. Flat-out, this model will do 199 mph (320 kph). As for the maximum output and thrust, they are rated at 792 hp (590 kW/802 ps) and 1,055 lb-ft (1,430 Nm), and while the former number is inferior, the latter is superior compared to this modded GT 63 S.
Photo: Instagram | performmaster In addition to the modified oily bits, the pictured Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S also has a few extras on the outside. PerformMaster mentions the front splitter with flaps on the sides, as well as the rear spoiler, and the rear diffuser, and to no one’s surprise, they have been made of carbon fiber. The usual black elements contrast this car’s satin blue exterior, and the vehicle rides on what seem to be the standard wheels, and they feature a bi-tone look. There are also some chrome bits and pieces on deck, too.
A look inside would have been great, but the tuner hasn’t opened the door of this ride, at the time of writing, anyway. And this likely means that the interior hasn’t been modified at all. Due to the angles, we cannot really see it by zooming in through the windows in some images, but in my vision, this thing would look best with black leather upholstery, and Alcantara on the pillars and headliner, as well as the usual amount of carbon fiber trim.
Now, PerformMaster hasn’t said anything about the pricing of this tuning bundle, so we do not know how much you will have to fork out if you want your very own Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S to be this punchy, and look the same with the carbon extras. Thus, interested parties much reach out to the tuner. But if you owned such a thing, would you really have it modified, or would you stick to the standard power and look? 2027 Hot Wheels Case C Unboxing: Aston Martin Super Treasure Hunt Is Coming Soon
56 photos
Photo: eBay/User Theoriginsdotcom
It can sometimes be quite complicated to keep up with all the Hot Wheels news. There’s always a new color variation, wheel change, new casting, packaging or even a new series to look at (think Racing Culture for 2027). And I’m sure Mattel has by no means exhausted all of the ideas for future releases.
Just think about it, the company can dig through over a century of automotive history and culture. It’s not just about the car manufacturers, but also about the tuners, racing teams, designers and people involved in the industry.
Of course going all out and creating all new models each year, without any repeats or color variations wouldn’t be feasible though.
We could probably go on like that for a few years, but the licensing fees would probably be insane, enough to even jeopardize the current status of the multi-billion dollar toy empire.
Anyway, I’m just here to show you what’s coming up in the third Mainline case for 2027, and I’m fairly certain you’ve never seen some of the cars inside.
Regular Treasure Hunt Photo: Done Teka Let’s start with the new regular Treasure Hunt model, the GT Hunter. It’s the third original casting for the TH series next year, which means we migh have to endure two more of them before a licensed design shows up.
At least that’s what it was like in 2026, when the 2 Jet Z, Total Disposal, Amaru GTC, Sweet Drive and Mad Manga preceded the Ford Model A Custom ‘31. You could say the GT Hunter is the fourth such item in a row, considering the 2026 series will conclude with the Gazella GT.
The GT Hunter is Ryu Asada’s creation from the 2015 HW Race: HW Race Team mini-series, and I think I remember seeing it in toy stores at the time. Mattel even used it for a Valentino Rossi tribute set in 2018, predating a short incursion into the ID series where it had three variations between 2019 and 2021.
The 2023 Neon Speeders release was one of its few memorable appearances after that, and I didn’t think it would ever return to the Mainline collection. The red, green and yellow color combo isn’t half bad and kids might just enjoy playing with it once it arrives in toy stores.
Super Treasure Hunt Photo: eBay/User STH Sales Almost two months have passed since we saw the first preview of the Aston Martin DBS Safari Edition, so we knew it was coming. I think that up until now the general consensus was that the third Super Treasure Hunt for 2027 would be the ‘87 Dodge D100, though.
I didn’t see it inside this case, whereas the basic version of the DBS is here complete with a Metalflake Green finish and black 5-spoke rims. While I enjoy the color combo on the STH, I’m not a fan of the Double 7-Spoke Real Riders it’s rolling on.
That hasn’t stopped some people on eBay from listing this collectible for as much as $200 (short card) on eBay, while the cheapest carded one has an asking price of just $70 (long card).
This is the second ever Aston Martin to join the Super Treasure Hunt ranks in 19 years since Mattel introduced the concept in its current form. The Aston Martin DB4GT High-Speed Edition came first in 2025, and here I am hoping the Valkyrie will make the switch from Elite 64 to the Mainline or Premium collections soon.
Case C Highlights Photo: Done Teka You might remember that I showed you a preview of Case B roughly three weeks ago. Seeing collectibles from that mix in this new one is common practice for Mattel, and it makes perfect sense for those which are typically in high demand from enthusiasts worldwide.
I’m talking about cars like the Ferrari F2004, the red Honda Civic Type R EK9, the 2019 Audi TT Safari, the BMW M4 GT3 (which was Case B’s Super Treasure Hunt) and a few other items you’ll spot inside the photo gallery.
With that in mind, let’s figure out what’s new. I assume many people have been eagerly waiting for the Police-spec Nissan Skyline GT-R (BNR34), and it’s honestly a bit underwhelming at this point. I don’t remember seeing the Cadillac Formula 1 Team race car before though.
It comes right after Ralf Schumacher pointed out Valtteri Bottas should walk away from the sport, making way for Esteban Ocon.
Photo: Done Teka I haven’t watched F1 in quite some time, but I don’t think fans have ever admire Ocon as much as they have the Finnish driver. However, I realize scoring more (or should I say some) points is a major concern for the American team, as Marcin Budkowski’s squad hasn’t been off to a promising debut.
I’m currently thinking about buying this year’s Japanese Car Culture Themed Multipack, which is essentially a Silver Series release featuring the Nissan Patrol Custom alongside five other vehicles.
It’s easily the best variation of this machine so far, and it’s good to know we can look forward to two of them in 2027. This HW Dirt version features a Metalflake Silver finish and the same wheels Dmitriy Shakhmatov’s casting has been using since its 2023 debut.
I’d buy for the Michelin decals, and I recommend zooming in if you didn’t spot them the first time around. The Quinjet is brand-new for 2027, and I’m surprised it’s joining the Mainline first and not Pop Culture.
Photo: Done Teka Bryan Zhao’s design is headed straight for the Screen Time mini-collection, and we currently don’t have any information about the other nine items that it will be joining there.
I don’t plan on watching Avengers: Doomsday, which means I also don’t really care about the Quinjet either. The Braille Racer Deora II is also new for next year, and it’s simply amazing to see how this concept has evolved over the decades.
The original Deora has been around since 1968, and it’s probably safe to say that it’s even more popular than the Bone Shaker. You can’t say the same thing about the Blitzspeeder yet, as it’s only about a decade old at this point.
It had a pink tinted canopy the last time we saw it in 2025, and you might like to know it was part of the Treasure Hunt series in 2018. If you think things have become repetitive over in Fast and Furious land, then look at what’s going on with Batman -themed collectibles.
Photo: Done Teka It’s not likely the team in El Segundo plans to retire the TV Series Batmobile anytime soon, and I imagine some enthusiasts might actually enjoy buying more of them year in and year out.
This Twin Mill variation is new for Case C and it’s amazing to think Ira Gilford’s casting is nearing its 60th anniversary. This is its first Mainline appearance since 2022, which means it might not be easy to find one in the wild.
If you’ve seen any of my Hot Wheels preview stories before, the yellow Maserati Tipo 61 won’t surprise you. I’m happy to explore this era via the 1/64th-scale replicas coming from El Segundo, as even finding these cars in a museum could be tricky if you don’t live in “the right” country.
The third variation of the Twin Tags features the return of the Aerodisc wheels. It’s the kind of design that’s not just a toy, as it can also work as a key ring or luggage tag if you don’t mind people calling you a geek afterward.
Photo: Done Teka Seeing the Track Dwagon on 3-spoke wheels reminds me of the Nissan Maxima Drift Car, and I would always go with the latter if I had to choose between them.
Seeing the 2020 Koenigsegg Jesko again is almost amusing to me now, having discovered the Tarmac Works CC850 and Gemera castings. Yes, I realize those are in a different price league, but you definitely get what you pay for.
Once you look past the Hako Type D, the Nissan Skyline H/T 2000 GT-R and the Datsun Sunny Coupe, you might realize the 2019 Jeep Grand Cherokee Trackhawk is new to the Mainline collection.
I should’ve seen it coming, as this year’s Performance Trucks version had a plastic base despite using Silver Series wheels. I assume it arrived to this point after failing to deliver as a Premium-exclusive collectible since its 2021 debut. I’ll be back with a review for Case D in three to four weeks from now!

Borderlands Mexico is a weekly rundown of developments in the world of United States-Mexico cross-border trucking and trade. This week in Borderlands Mexico: Avocado imports generate $641M for US trucking, warehousing; GLS US expands parcel delivery network to Texas border market and Jetco expands heavy-haul operations to serve Gulf Coast industrial boom.
Avocado imports generate $641M for US trucking, warehousing
Mexican Hass avocado imports generated an estimated $641.5 million in U.S. transportation and warehousing activity and supported more than 4,150 jobs in fiscal year 2025-26.
The findings by Texas A&M University researchers highlight the growing importance of cross-border trucking, refrigerated transportation and distribution networks connecting Mexican agricultural producers with U.S. consumers.
The report, The U.S. Economic Contributions of Hass Avocado Imports from Mexico , was prepared by Gary W. Williams, an emeritus professor in Texas A&M’s Department of Agricultural Economics, and Dan Hanselka, an extension program specialist.
Nearly 98% of Mexican avocados entering the U.S. in 2024 were transported by truck through Texas land ports, primarily through Pharr and Laredo .
The analysis, released Wednesday by the Avocado Institute of Mexico, estimated that Mexican Hass avocado imports generated $7.1 billion in total U.S. economic output and supported 37,163 jobs across multiple industries during the fiscal year ending June 2026.
Texas plays a central role in transporting Mexican avocados to U.S. markets.
According to USDA data cited in the Texas A&M report, the Pharr border crossing handled approximately 58.2% of Mexican avocado imports in 2024, while Laredo accounted for another 39.4%.
Once shipments clear the border, avocados move through an extensive network of trucking companies, refrigerated warehouses, wholesalers, distribution centers and food processors before reaching grocery stores, restaurants and other customers nationwide.
The report found that avocado shipments generate additional economic activity through purchases of fuel, equipment, transportation services, repairs and other logistics-related services.
The economic contributions extend beyond companies directly transporting the fruit, supporting businesses throughout interconnected supply chains.
In Texas alone, an estimated $245.1 million in Mexican Hass avocado imports generated $428.9 million in economic output, contributed $265.5 million to the state’s gross domestic product and supported 2,402 jobs across industries.
The study estimated that California, the nation’s largest avocado-consuming state, generated $968.2 million in economic output and supported 5,325 jobs associated with Mexican avocado imports.
Together, Texas and California accounted for only 19% to 22% of the national economic contributions measured in the study, demonstrating how the supply chain extends throughout the country.
The Texas A&M analysis also found that $3.2 billion in Mexican Hass avocado imports during fiscal year 2025/26 contributed an estimated $4.4 billion to U.S. GDP.
The imports also supported $2.4 billion in labor income and generated approximately $1 billion in federal, state and local taxes.
“This report demonstrates the value of a deeply integrated North American supply chain built over decades between Mexico and the U.S.,” said Ron Campbell, executive director of the Mexican Hass Avocado Import Association, in a statement.
“Mexican avocados don’t simply cross the border, they generate economic activity throughout the U.S. economy, supporting transportation and distribution networks, retailers, restaurants and communities across the country.”
GLS US expands parcel delivery network to Texas border market
Regional parcel delivery provider GLS US has expanded its services into El Paso, Texas, strengthening its shipping network across the Western U.S and adding another market along the U.S.–Mexico border.
The expansion, announced Oct. 20, gives businesses in West Texas access to first-, middle- and final-mile delivery services. The new location also can determine international shipping capabilities and parcel transportation for shipments weighing up to 150 pounds.
El Paso is a major U.S.–Mexico trade gateway, supported by manufacturing, distribution and cross-border commerce with neighboring Ciudad Juárez, Mexico.
GLS said its expanded network will serve manufacturers, distributors, retailers and e-commerce businesses seeking improved shipping connectivity throughout Texas and the Western U.S.
The move into El Paso follows GLS US’s expansion into Houston, Austin and San Antonio earlier this year, after entering the Dallas-Fort Worth market in 2025.
GLS US is part of GLS Group, a European parcel delivery company operating in more than 50 countries and handling more than 900 million parcels annually.
Jetco expands heavy-haul operations to serve Gulf Coast boom
Houston-based trucking and logistics provider Jetco has launched a specialized cargo division aimed at growing demand for heavy-haul transportation tied to data centers, power generation, manufacturing and infrastructure projects along the Gulf Coast.
The division combines Jetco’s existing heavy-haul operations, established in 2008, with its expanding freight brokerage business to handle oversized, overweight and over-dimensional cargo.
“Three years ago, we started positioning ourselves to capitalize on the accelerated growth of domestic power, manufacturing, and infrastructure, specifically data centers,” Jetco President Kyle Kristynik said in a statement.
The company has added four specialized trailers this year, including two Faymonville multimax trailers capable of hauling 125,000 pounds each, a Goldhofer trailer rated for 180,000 pounds and a Fontaine hydraulic removable gooseneck trailer with a 55-ton capacity in a 16-foot footprint.
Jetco said the division will combine its own trucks and trailers with prequalified third-party carriers to manage complex industrial shipments.
The company also plans to collaborate with Canadian sister companies Precision Specialized and Scott Woods Transport to support specialized, heavy-haul and out-of-gauge freight movements.
Jetco, which is part of Canadian transportation company The GTI Group, operates from its Houston headquarters and maintains facilities in Pasadena, Freeport and Dallas, Texas.
Why it matters: The report “The U.S. Economic Contributions of Hass Avocado Imports from Mexico,” highlights how Mexican agricultural imports sustain U.S. trucking jobs, refrigerated distribution networks and freight activity far beyond the border .

5 Impressive Yet Grossly Underrated Hot Hatches From the 1980s
11 photos
Photo: Stellantis N.V.
The 1980s was an exciting decade for factory-built performance. More and more fast versions of mass-produced hatchbacks began appearing and even the term “hot hatch” itself was coined during that memorable period. But while several iconic hot hatches form the 1980s are still revered by enthusiasts to this day, there are some brilliant machines that remain grossly underrated.
The term “hot hatch” began gaining traction during the second part of the 1980s, with more and more wild, motorsport-derived models being lunched.
Among those were the likes of the Renault 5 Turbo 2, MG Metro 6R4 or Peugeot 205 Turbo 16, three mid-engined legends born out of the highly-competitive Group B rally category.
Apart from those race cars for the road, more conventional performance models like the Peugeot 205 GTi, Volkswagen Golf GTI Mk 2, or the Lancia Delta HF Integrale also became icons of the 1980s, solidifying their place in automotive history books.
Nevertheless, several other hot hatches born during that decade didn’t exactly become legendary, despite being impressive performance machines. In following paragraphs, we’re going to rediscover five of these grossly underrated models and remember what made them spectacular.
1983 Fiat Ritmo/Strada Abarth 130 TC Photo: Stellantis N.V. Though Abarth gained worldwide fame during the 1980s for its collaboration with Lancia on models such as the Rally 037 or the Delta S4, the company also helped Fiat develop performance-oriented that attempted to go head-to-head with VW’s popular Golf GTI .
Unveiled at the 1981 Frankfurt Motor Show as the Ritmo Abarth 125 TC, the performance-oriented Abarth version based on the Fiat Ritmo (aka Strada) was improved as part of the second series revamp in 1982,
Debuting in 1982 as a 1983 model, the Abarth 130 TC wasn’t much different from other Ritmo versions, with only a rear spoiler and bespoke wheels hinting at its sporty nature.
Photo: Stellantis N.V. Powered by a 2.0-liter Lampredi DOHC eight-valve four-cylinder rated at 128 hp, the hot hatch was praised for its handling, which resulted from the stiffer Abarh-tuned suspension.
With that massive 2.0-liter mated to a close-ratio five-speed manual, the 130 TC felt far livelier and far more thrilling to drive than any other Ritmo/Stada.
Unfortunately, the model failed to become as popular as it should’ve been, mainly because of fierce competition from more renowned rivals like the Golf GTI or the Peugeot 205 GTi.
1986 Shelby Omni GLH-S Photo: Mecum Auctions While not as popular as the were in Europe, hot hatches managed to find their niche in the US during the 1980s with models like the Golf GTI and Civic Si selling well nationwide.
Sensing the opportunity, the Chrysler Corporation partnered with the legendary Carroll Shelby and created a performance-oriented version of the Dodge Omni called GLH (Goes Like Hell).
While that model was pretty interesting, Shelby took it to another level in 1986 when he purchased 500 units and transformed them into the first Shelby-badged hot hatch ever produced, the GLH-S (Goes Like Hell S'more).
The Shelby GLH-S benefited from a long list of upgrades, including bespoke wheels, a revamped suspension system and a more powerful engine.
Photo: Mecum Auctions That engine was the same Chrysler 2.2-liter turbocharged inline-four that powered the Omni GLH, but thanks to extensive tuning, which included an intercooler, a larger turbo and a modified throttle body, output rose from 146 to 175 hp.
The GLH-S was capable of accelerating from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 6.5 seconds and ran the quarter mile in 14.8 seconds, which made it extremely impressive for its era.
Nevertheless, a high sticker price combined with no serious motorsport involvement and lack of availability outside the US limited its potential.
Now often forgotten, the Shelby Omni GLH-S remains one of the most underrated hot hatches of the 1980s and one of the most underrated American performance cars of all time.
1986 Lancia Delta HF 4WD Photo: Stellantis N.V. When it comes to iconic hot hatches, few are more highly-regarded than the Delta HF Integrale , which was one of the most dominant ranges of rally cars and road-legal homologation specials of all time.
However, enthusiasts often forget about its immediate predecessor, the Delta HF 4WD. Unveiled at the Turin Motor Show in the spring of 1986, this version saw Lancia concentrate the bulk of its rally efforts on the Group A regulations, since the wild Group B got banned due to serious accidents.
Nearly identical in appearance to the standard Delta, the HF 4WD was a completely different machine, since it debuted a new permanent four-wheel-drive system based on the one used in the mid-engine Delta S4.
Photo: Stellantis N.V. Apart from the 4WD system, the model got several other upgrades, including a DOHC 2.0-liter turbocharged inline-four that featured a Garrett turbo and an air-to-air intercooler.
Rated at 165 hp, the engine allowed the car to sprint to 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill in 7.5 seconds and, combined with the improved suspension and 4WD system, made it one of the most thrilling to drive hot hatches of the era.
While the formula was further refined in the Inegrale Deltas that followed, the less-glamorous, often-forgotten HF 4WD remains one of the most exciting hot hatches of the decade.
1987 Citroen BX GTi 16v Photo: Stellantis N.V. Originally introduced in 1982, the BX was the successor of the successful GS/GSA range. During its lifespan, it was available in various performance versions, with the most impressive being launched in 1987.
Dubbed GTi 16v, the model became the pinnacle of BX performance and differed from its rivals due to its lack of forced induction .
Like the name implies, the BX GTi 16v was powered by a 16-valve 1.9-liter inline-four that made a healthy 158 hp without the use of a turbo or supercharger.
Photo: Stellantis N.V. Apart from that impressive engine, the BX GTi 16v featured distinch styling upgrades that made it look more aggressive and also came with Citroen’s advanced hydropneumatics suspension that made it one of the best-handling hot hatches of the era.
Able to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 7.6 seconds, the GTi 16v was as potent as many of its direct rivals, but failed to become as popular as it should’ve been mainly due to limited motorsport involvement and Citroen’s image as a manufacturer of comfort-oriented models, rather than performance cars .
Despite being often forgotten and still grossly underated, the BX GTi 16v remains one of the most impressive hot hatches of the 1980s.
1989 Volkswagen Golf Rallye G60 Photo: Volkswagen Golf Rallye G60 The original Golf GTI is widely credited for kickstarting the hot hatch segment back in 1975. Extremely popular, the performance-oriented Golf returned as part of the Mk2 lineup and continued to be one of the most highly-regarded models of its kind.
However, enthusiasts often forget that the most impressive Mk2 Golf was not the GTI. That title goes to the Rallye G60, a limited-edition variant launched in 1989 to homologate the Golf for Group A rally competitions.
Unlike the GTI, the Rallye was equipped with a bespoke body kit that made it look far more aggressive.
Photo: Volkswagen Golf Rallye G60 Mechanically, it came with VW’s Syncro four-wheel drive system, special suspension tuning, and was powered by a 1.8-liter four-cylinder rated at 160 hp courtesy of a G-Lader scroll-type volumetric supercharger.
The Rallye looked more aggressive and was more capable than the GTI, but, due to the fact that it cost roughly twice as much and it failed to be a resounding success in full rally trim, the model failed to reach the same heights of popularity as the GTI.
The Golf Rallye G60 was produced in a run of 5,000 units of which a surprisingly low number of cars are still around.
Though it failed to become an icon of the 1980s, the model remains one of the most exciting hot hatches developed in Europe during that decade.

5 Spectacular Wagons That Went From Family Haulers to Motorsport Stars
15 photos
Photo: Subaru
Throughout the decades, motorsport competitions that run cars heavily based on production models have seen several pretty unconventional machines being entered. Among those unconventional machines were the following five wagons which deserve to be revisited.
When choosing a car for a competition that features production models, racing teams often go with the lightest, most aerodynamically-efficient available.
Of course, wagons, which often have been developed for purely practical reasons, have rarely been the go-to option to base a race car on.
Nevertheless, on some occasions these family haulers have been adapted for the track and we’re going to revisit five of the most spectacular.
Volvo 850 Estate Photo: Volvo The 850 was introduced by Volvo in 1991 as a 1992 model. Available as a sedan or as a wagon, the model carried Volvo’s traditional boxy styling, but with subtle curves that made it distinctly more modern than the 240, its long-serving predecessor.
The 850 came with many new features for a Volvo , such as a transversally-mounted five-cylinder engine, front wheel drive, a Delta-link rear axle, or a side impact protection system.
Produced until the end of the 1997 model year, the 850 proved to be successful, selling in over 700,000 units worldwide.
Photo: Volvo In an effort to promote the model and improve its conservative image, Volvo made the wild decision to enter the 1994 British Touring Car Championship (BTCC) with an 850 wagon, rather than a sedan.
Prepped and ran by motorsport experts, Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR) , the two 850 wagons debuted in April 1994 at the season opener in Thruxton and went on to compete in every race that season.
In terms of results, the Swedish wagons never won a race and a fifth overall finish at Oulton Park and Snetterton were their best results.
Despite that, the Volvo 850 Estate was a huge hit with the fans and remains one of the most iconic cars to ever compete in the BTCC.
MG ZT-T Photo: MG Introduced in 2001, the ZT sedan and its wagon sibling, the ZT-T were developed as an attempt by MG Rover to revive interest in the MG brand .
Based on, and nearly identical in terms of aesthetics with the Rover 75, the ZT and ZT-T enjoyed moderate success and survived on the market until the end of the 2005 model year.
Available in several trims with a wide range of engine choices, the ZT-T went down as a well-built wagon that some Brittons chose as their main family car.
Photo: MG In the fall of 2003, MG decided to promote its wagon in a pretty unconventional way and modified one into a full race car that aimed to become the world’s fastest wagon.
MG Rover’s then design director, Peter Stevens, the man who also worked on the McLaren F1 coordinated the project, which saw a production ZT-T being modified by So-Cal Speed Shop into a record-braking monster.
Powered by a Roush Performance -developed 6.0-liter V8 rated at around 800 hp, this wagon-turned-race car managed to set a new speed record at 55th annual Bonneville Speed Week Nationals, achieving a top speed of 225.609 mph (360.9 kph) and becoming the World's Fastest (non-production) wagon.
Honda Civic Tourer Photo: Honda Produced from 2011 to 2017, the ninth-generation of the legendary Honda Civic wasn’t the most memorable in terms of styling, but remains highly-regarded by the brand’s enthusiasts, particularly in Type R guise.
But while all Honda enthusiasts remember the Type R , few think about the wagon when the ninth-generation Civic is mentioned.
The wagon, marketed as the Civic Tourer, was introduced in concept form at the 2013 Geneva Motor Show and went into production about a year later.
Photo: Honda Partially because Honda wanted to promote the wagon, and partially because three-time BTCC champion Matt Neal wanted a new challenge, the Japanese carmaker’s works racing squad, Team Dynamics, decided to enter a Civic Tourer into the BTCC for the 2014 season.
Modified to full race guise, the Civic Tourer made its debut during the opening round at Brands Hatch and instantly became a fan-favorite.
Over the course of the season, it proved way more competitive than the Volvo 850 Estate, as it went on to win three races and finished in the top five on 23 occasions.
Like the Volvo, the Civic Tourer remains one of the most spectacular cars to ever race a full BTCC season, proving that a family hauler could successfully transition into motorsports.
Subaru Levorg Photo: Subaru The Levorg debuted in 2014 as the new-age successor of the Subaru Legacy wagon. Based on the same platform as the Impreza/WRX and the Legacy, it shared visual cues with both and was only available with a CVT transmission and all-wheel drive.
Its name came from a blend of three words: LEgacy, reVOlution and touring and it was reasonably successful, surviving on the market until 2020, when it was replaced by the heavily updated second generation.
Conceived as a sporty-looking wagon with solid capabilities, it was available with one of three flat-four engines, the most potent of which being capable of delivering 296 hp.
Photo: Subaru In 2016, Subaru announced it was entering the BTCC with partners Team BMR, surprising everyone by choosing the Levorg as its challenger.
The competition cars were heavily modified, gaining a Mountune Racing-prepped version of the powerful FA20 2.0-liter boxer and a conversion to RWD.
The Levorg’s debut season wasn’t terrific, but things changed in the following season when the wagon driven by Ash Sutton won the BTCC Drivers' Championship.
The Levorg competed in four full seasons and apart from the 2017 Drivers' Championship, it racked up no less than 21 race wins, which made it the most successful wagon in motorsport history.
BMW M3 Touring 24H Photo: BMW AG The current G80/G81 BMW M3 was unveiled in 2020 and while its controversial front end got a lot of hate, nobody complained about the Bavarian carmaker’s decision to finally produce an M3 in wagon guise.
Marketed as the M3 Touring , the high-performance wagon was met with universal praise by the public and the press, and has been selling well since a surprising number of enthusiasts realized that the combination of practicality and performance is just too good to pass up.
The M3 Touring didn’t need much advertising to sell well, but despite that, BMW decided to promote their practical powerhouse by developing a race version and entering it in the epic Nürburgring 24-hour race.
Photo: BMW AG It all started last year (2025) when BMW’s M division published a series of digital renderings of a race-ready M3 Touring. But, since those images were published on April 1st, everyone thought it was a prank.
The story goes that it was indeed a prank, but due to the overwhelmingly positive reaction, the M division’s engineers went ahead and actually built a race-ready M3 Touring.
The car was entered in this year’s edition of the grueling 24-hour race with thorough modifications and all the race hardware of its M4 GT3 EVO sibling. It finished the race 5th overall and 1st in the SPX class.

He recently took upon himself to redesign the G50 BMW 3 Series, the M350 xDrive to be more precise, in an unofficial, hypothetical design project. His idea was simple: he used the Neue Klasse illuminated kidneys from the latest X5 along with dual round LED surround daytime running lights and bigger plus shorter LED taillights to reference the legendary E30 BMW M3 coupe classic allure. Then he also went overboard with a CGI BMW M3 with all-yellow LED lights at the front and a bonkers aerodynamic package, of course.
But now he’s relaxed once again, and claims that “one of the most beautiful bodies BMW had” was the GT variant of its main BMW 5, 6, and 3 Series – which is a point of contention, since a lot of people would also argue that they were, in fact, some of the ugliest versions. Anyway, beauty is always in the eye of the beholder, and the pixel master wants to bring back the discontinued body style.
As such, his latest vision regarding the BMW 3 Series this time around has to do with a digital remake of the BMW 3 Series GT. He deployed the round headlights with LED ‘angel eye’ daytime running lamps from the M350 xDrive and also put a wide kidney grille, which is also functional since this is a 340i version, then added the sloping roof from the iX4 coupe- SUV model and, around the back, put a new trunk lid stolen from the 6 GT with slimmer full-width lights.
